title: PFRDA Finalises NPS Swasthya: 25% Medical Withdrawal Cap, Health Cover Up to Rs 30 Lakh
excerpt: The pension regulator's September 18 guidelines spell out how much NPS Swasthya subscribers can draw for healthcare, the mandatory four-tier family-floater insurance, and what happens if a renewal premium goes unpaid.
body:
• PFRDA's September 18 guidelines cap NPS Swasthya healthcare withdrawals at 25% of the subscriber's contributions, with payouts settled directly with hospitals and no limit on the number of withdrawals.
  • The scheme bundles retirement savings with a mandatory family-floater super top-up policy offering up to ₹30 lakh of cover (₹3 lakh deductible), covering the subscriber, spouse and two dependent children.
  • If the renewal premium goes unpaid and the cover lapses, the Swasthya account is closed and merged into a standard All Citizen NPS account; entry age is 18–70 with renewals to 85.

The pension regulator has put a final frame around one of its most closely watched experiments. On September 18, the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) issued the operational guidelines for NPS Swasthya, the healthcare-linked variant of the National Pension System that pairs retirement savings with a mandatory health insurance cover — and fixed the rules on how much subscribers can actually draw when medical bills arrive.

The headline number: subscribers can withdraw up to 25% of their contributions to the NPS Swasthya account for eligible outpatient and inpatient healthcare expenses, with no cap on the number of withdrawals and no minimum waiting period prescribed by the regulator. Payouts are not handed to the subscriber — they are settled directly with the hospital or healthcare provider.

How the scheme works

NPS Swasthya emerged from a proof-of-concept run under PFRDA's regulatory sandbox in early 2026, built for a familiar Indian problem: retirement savings locked away while medical costs rise 11.5–14% a year. The final design keeps two legally and operationally separate components — an investment account, and a mandatory super top-up health insurance policy.

"The insurance structure comes in four tiers: a ₹10,000 deductible unlocks ₹1 lakh of cover, ₹50,000 unlocks ₹5 lakh, ₹1 lakh unlocks ₹10 lakh, and ₹3 lakh unlocks ₹30 lakh."

The insurance structure comes in four tiers: a ₹10,000 deductible unlocks ₹1 lakh of cover, ₹50,000 unlocks ₹5 lakh, ₹1 lakh unlocks ₹10 lakh, and ₹3 lakh unlocks ₹30 lakh. The family floater covers the subscriber, spouse and up to two dependent children. Entry is open from age 18 to 70, with renewals possible up to age 85. There is a 30-day initial waiting period (except for accidents) and a 12-month wait for pre-existing and specified diseases.

What a lapsed premium costs

The guidelines also spell out the stick behind the mandatory insurance. If the balance is insufficient for the renewal premium, the pension fund must alert the subscriber at 90, 60 and 30 days before renewal. If the premium still goes unpaid after the grace period and the cover lapses, the Swasthya account is closed and merged into an ordinary All Citizen Model NPS account — the healthcare access disappears.

On the contribution side, the minimum initial payment equals the first-year insurance premium (including taxes), plus a ₹200 annual health-benefit-administrator maintenance charge, plus at least ₹1,000 of investment. Subsequent contributions can be as low as ₹10, and the pension fund's management fee on the Swasthya corpus is capped at 0.08% a year. Existing NPS (All Citizen) funds can be transferred in, limited to meeting the applicable insurance deductible.

For catastrophic bills, a premature-exit provision lets a subscriber deploy the accumulated corpus when a single inpatient bill exceeds what a partial withdrawal can reach — an acknowledgement that 25% of contributions may not cover a major hospitalisation.

Who it is for — and the open questions

The scheme's stated audience is people who cannot afford hefty standalone health premiums, giving them a regulated route to retirement savings that can also absorb medical shocks. For NRIs planning a retirement in India, the product is worth watching — though the guidelines' eligibility details for non-residents were not spelled out in the published reports, and that detail matters before anyone plans around it.

Two ambiguities remain. The February proof-of-concept circular had required a ₹50,000 minimum corpus before the first withdrawal; the final-guidelines reporting does not mention it — whether the condition was dropped or simply omitted from coverage is unclear. The premature-exit trigger is also described slightly differently across documents. Until PFRDA's full circular text is parsed line by line, subscribers should treat the press summaries as the shape of the rules, not the letter.

What's next

With the framework finalised, the execution now falls to the pension funds, TPAs and insurers running the scheme. The real test will be claims experience: whether the 25% cap plus super top-up is enough for serious illnesses, and whether the premium-lapse rule pushes subscribers out of the healthcare component just when they need it. The first renewal cycle will tell.
